extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate and advanced high-school students studying enumerative combinatorics / math-olympiad contestants
extracted.subtask_description: Solve and justify enumerative-combinatorics problems: derive recurrences and closed forms, construct bijections and combinatorial proofs, apply PIE, and translate combinatorial constraints into countable structures (paths, trees, placements, tournaments, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Find a recursion and a formula for f(n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive a recurrence relation satisfied by f(n) and provide an explicit (closed-form) formula for f(n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify initial conditions, form the recurrence by partitioning cases (e.g., by first term, last operation, or position), solve the characteristic equation for linear recurrences, and determine constants from initial values. Example: Problem 16 gives f(n)=2f(n−1)+2f(n−2) with f(0)=1,f(1)=3 and instructs to solve the characteristic equation λ^2−2λ−2=0 to get a closed form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret occurrences of Catalan numbers as 'good paths'
rubrics_metrics.description: When Catalan numbers arise, give a bijective interpretation in terms of 'good paths' (Dyck-path-like lattice walks) or equivalent objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate the combinatorial object (nonintersecting chords, triangulations, parenthesizations, binary trees) into well-formed lattice paths (steps right/up with constraints). Example: Problem 18 maps nonintersecting chord pairings to words of b/e and then to good paths; Problems 19–21 connect triangulations and parenthesizations to Catalan numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bijection or double-counting (counting same objects two ways)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove combinatorial identities by constructing explicit bijections between sets or by counting the same family of objects in two different ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the mapping is one-to-one (or give inverse) for bijections; for double-counting, partition counts by a parameter and equate two expressions. The text explicitly instructs this for Problem 22 and uses it in many solutions (committee & chairman, subset/complement arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Principle of Inclusion–Exclusion (PIE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use PIE to count objects subject to forbidden properties by counting complements and alternating sums of intersections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up Ai as the set violating a given property (e.g., divisible by prime pi or a mapping missing some target) and compute |⋃Ai| via inclusion-exclusion. Examples: Problem 27 (Euler φ-function) and Problem 28 (number of surjections s(m,n)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive recurrences by considering insertion of an extra element
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain recurrences for permutation/enumeration-type numbers, consider adding element n+1 and analyze whether it forms a new cycle/fixed point or is inserted into existing structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count cases where the new element is isolated vs. integrated, multiply by number of insertion positions if needed. Example: Problem 26 gives F(n+1,r)=F(n,r−1)+nF(n,r) for Stirling numbers of the first kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate constrained selections into gap/placement problems (stars-and-bars style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model selections with adjacency or spacing constraints by representing chosen items as objects placed into allowed 'slots' or gaps, then count choices of slots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common for counting k-subsets with no neighbors: reduce to choosing positions among available gaps. Example: Problem 25 counts 6-subsets with no neighbors on 49 numbers by selecting 6 places from 44 available positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count parenthesizations via recursive decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Count ways to place parentheses in a product of n factors by decomposing at the last multiplication and summing over possible split points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write an = Σ_{k=1}^{n−1} a_k a_{n−k} with base cases; recognize the Catalan recurrence and connect to triangulations and binary trees (Problems 20–21).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish one-to-one correspondences between structures (trees, paths, triangulations)
rubrics_metrics.description: When counting, exhibit explicit bijections among parenthesizations, binary trees, triangulations, Dyck paths, and noncrossing partitions to transfer known counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the mapping (e.g., parentheses → path by reading opens as right, variables as up) and prove it's bijective. Used to show counts equal Catalan numbers (Problems 19–21).

rubrics_metrics.name: Solve linear recurrences using characteristic equations
rubrics_metrics.description: For linear constant-coefficient recurrences, derive the characteristic polynomial, find roots, and write the general term as linear combination of powers; determine coefficients from initial values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Fibonacci-style recurrences (Problems 7, 16, 31–32) and recurrences with λ^2−2λ−2 etc. Use initial values to get constants a,b.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use casework on a distinguished element (first/last/endpoint) to split counting
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition the set of objects by the behavior or position of a particular distinguished element (e.g., first child, first digit, first summand) and sum counts over cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical approach for recurrences and combinatorial sums: e.g., Problems 16 (words starting with certain prefixes), 31 (children seats, split by where first child goes), 30 (packing k successive points with endpoint vs. non-endpoint cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use symmetry and complement arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit symmetry (complements, reversing, labeling invariance) to simplify counting and reduce cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include mapping subset ↔ complement in binomial identities (Problem 22b), counting unordered pairs from ordered counts (Problem 13), and halving symmetric counts (even/odd subsets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parity/counting contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply parity (odd/even) arguments to show impossibility or derive contradictions by counting multiplicities modulo 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Problem 34 shows a polyhedron with faces all odd leads to contradiction because sum of face-edge counts is odd but twice number of edges must be even.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encode combinatorial constraints as state machines/graphs and read recurrences from transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent allowed local transitions between symbols/states as a directed graph; derive linear recurrences for counts from adjacency transitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read off recurrences from the graph's transition rules (Problems 38 and 39 show deriving xn, yn via state graphs and converting to single recurrence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Count via algebraic/product expansions mapping to subsets
rubrics_metrics.description: Expand a product ∏(1+term_i) to get a sum indexed by subsets, interpreting each summand as contribution of that subset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to sum reciprocals over all nonempty subsets by expanding ∏_{i=1}^n (1+1/i) (Problem 37). Throw away the empty-set term if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design minimal tournament/selection procedures via knockout (pairwise elimination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model selection of top-ranked elements by knockout tournaments: each match eliminates one candidate; count matches needed and analyze candidates for subsequent ranks among those who lost to the winner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For n players, n−1 games find the winner; to find top k, use rounds among those who lost to top players. Examples: Problems 23, 40–42 explaining counts like 127+6+6=139 for top 3 among 128.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count using combinatorial inversion/inequality solving for positional sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: When enumerating sequences built with growing multiplicities (k appears k times), invert triangular-number inequalities to find which k corresponds to position n and express closed form accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solve k(k−1)/2 < n ≤ k(k+1)/2 for k; use quadratic formula and rounding to nearest integer (Problem 29 gives two equivalent solutions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Count occurrences of a given term across all compositions by positional packing
rubrics_metrics.description: To count how many times a given part k appears across all compositions of n, encode compositions as n points with bars between gaps; count placements of a k-block (packed k consecutive points) and multiply by choices of bar placements, splitting endpoint vs non-endpoint cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 30: derive T(n,k)=(n−k+3)2^{n−k−2} by counting packed placements that contain an endpoint and those that do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct explicit constructive partitions/translates using positional/base representations
rubrics_metrics.description: When partitioning integers into infinite translates, give an explicit construction (e.g., using digits at even/odd positions in binary or positional constraints) showing each class is a translate of a fixed set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 35 constructs A as integers with zeros at even binary positions and B with zeros at odd positions, then forms translates A_k = A + b_k to partition N.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use elimination and reduction strategies in comparison-based selection problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce candidate set size by pairwise comparisons eliminating dominated elements; use divide-and-conquer comparisons to reduce to a small candidate set and finish with additional comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 36 describes eliminating large blocks of weights and then repeatedly halving the problem via comparisons (tournament-style elimination) to find the median with limited weighings.
